projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Lynden Levitt was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Lynden Levitt
sp.p: This interview is on the 26th day ofOctober 2002, at Midland, Michigan. The interview is being conducted by Carolyn Levitt, my granddaughter, ofChicago, and my name is Lynden D. Levitt, now living inMidland. My Navy serial number was 730-90-75. I'm now 77 years of age. My birth date was on January 21st --January, 1925, and I was ___+ was radioman first class, which was my basic training, but I was somewhat of a camouflage mate, but we'll go into that in the future when we talk a little bit further on about why it was that way. At the time that I had -- I beg your pardon? (Interviewer is inaudible throughout the entire recording.)

Yeah, I joined the Navy kind of uniquely. Didn't have any intention at the time. I was working at a defense job, making more money than I ever heard of in my life before. But ___+ Tillamook, Oregon working in a Naval air base along ways from home and got a letter one day from some people back home. And the letter just made reference to one fellow who had got his draft notice who I knew in town-- just happened to know him. And he was a young man but was married and had four kids. And he was drafted, and I couldn't believe it.

And that night I had gone -- I went to a movie in Tillamook, and the movie was China. And in this particular movie it depicted, presumably, the Rape of Nanking. I got so terribly incensed during the movie that I decided that night to join the Navy -- to leave, go back home and join the Navy and solve the problems of the world.

As a matter of fact, I quit the next day and did, in fact, immediately go back to Rapid City and join the Navy from there. I was 17 at that time. My initial service was at Great Lakes. That was where I was signed.

Oh, in joining the Navy, I knew so little about the Navy, actually, that's when I went down to enlist. They made reference to USNR, and the R kind of threw me. And they signed me up. In fact, they drew the initial enlistment document as USNR. And I caught it when I went to sign it, and I told him under no circumstances was I going to sign that because I wanted no part of the USNR. I didn't know what it meant by Ready Reserve because I was only 17. If I went in then, I would go in regular Navy. That's what I wanted, regular Navy.

So I signed up at the actual hitch on what they called a kiddie cruise which was I signed up until the day before I was 21. So when I went in, I went in USN like most guys went in and USNR. I rued that day, ultimately, but, you know, they made a couple three, four months difference in what service I was going to have anyhow.

Initial assignment was Great Lakes. And it was interesting because I really wasn't quite ready for military service it seems. I'd never been in such a regimented atmosphere. I still remember that my assignment was to Camp Moffett and -- there in Great Lakes. And when I went in, we were still what we called swinging hammocks. We didn't have bunk beds; we still had hammocks.

And during my would-be 30 days there, entered boot camp. We converted the hammocks and installed bunks, I think, which really slept there for one night. The people in the group that followed us used the bunks, but I went through boot camp in the old Navy swinging hammocks.

The chief in charge of our unit was a chief specialist. He was a former Chicago Cardinal tackle, and he had absolutely no more Navy experience than I did. Had absolutely no idea how to create a company. The only thing he knew how to do was to put us on the grinder every day and run. And that's what I did for every day I was in boot camp was to run. We'd go to breakfast and go out, and we would run. And this, of course -- after a while it became less than a joy and it'd be ___ time at that time, miserable climate there in Chicago.

And one day on a bulletin board someplace I saw a little notice about people that could play trumpets and becoming buglers. Well, that sounded like an awful lot more fun than running out on the grinder all day long. So another fellow and I followed -- went over to see a guy by the name of Franky -- I can still remember his name -- who was the bugler -- head bugler -- at Camp Moffett. We passed the test, too. We could both play trumpets, so we became immediate buglers.

I went back and told my chief that, and he had an absolute fit. There was no way he wanted anybody in his company to be a bugler. He wanted me to do exactly what everybody else did: standing watches, things of that nature. So I'm in immediate trouble with the chief, which got ___ of immediate extra duty, which went on for some short period of time until I told the captain of my company there is in Camp Moffett -- whose name was Mickey Cochrane -- that's Mickey Cochrane, a former catcher and who was a great, great guy. And at every inspection -- on Saturday inspection I would go over to his office, sit down and visit with him about baseball for a while, and be his bugler during inspection. And he protected me from my chief for a period of time at the end of my time there in boot camp.

I beg your pardon? Boot camp wasn't hard at all. It was just nothing but run the grinder. Just get out there and run and run and run all day long. It was not fun at all and terribly, terribly boring more than anything else. But also my company -- every company during the time they were there would be assigned KP duty. My company happened to catch KP duty the Christmas of 1943 because you'd get it for seven days. Because we caught Christmas they figured, well, why don't they also, rather than cooping two companies up for the holidays, just make one company do the Christmas and the New Year's. So we caught eight days and were unhappy about that situation. And I remember working in the bakery shop doing terrible. I mean, I wasn't really a baker at all -- doing janitor duties or things of that nature in the bakery shop.

One of the bakers was going out on leave one day -- one of the fellows that I worked with. And for some reason he's talking about buying liquor, and I mentioned it to some of the boys in my barracks -- about buying liquor. Now why this came about I really don't know because I wasn't any great drinker of hard liquor at that time, but to be able to have some sounded like a great deal on New Year's Eve. So I immediately grabbed as much money from friends of mine as I could get my hands on and gave it to this baker, and he was going to bring in as much liquor as that would buy. He did. He brought it in, and I think there was something like three or four quarts and one pint of whiskey that he got strapped to his legs and what have you, and he brought in through the gate -- back into Moffett for us.

I beg your pardon? Only 30 days. It was not -- so it worked out we got caught. We got caught with the liquor. And to make a long story short -- and I got court-martialed. I was in the Navy only 30 days and already I was on a captain's mast -- on a captain's mast because I admitted bringing the liquor in. And I swore that I drank it all because they were going through -- put my entire company on restriction, and they took one day away from my leave.

So, anyhow -- and also, to make things interesting, I get the German measles while I'm there. So I'm in the hospital for a week, and I thought they were going to holdme over, send me back through boots again but, fortunately, they didn't. And I was only in Great Lakes one week longer than normal because of the German measles.

While there, we took our classification exams, and from those exams they determined to send me -- they decided to send me on to radio school. So when I finished boots they give you a boot leave. As I said, I lost one day but -- and I was sent on to a radio school, and my radio school was at the University of Wisconsin at Madison.University of Wisconsin at that time was an absolutely ideal situation. It was early spring. We were quartered in Adams and Tripp Hall, two quadrangles that we took over. The food was outstanding, still remember it. The food was absolutely marvelous and right adjacent or not too far from the quadrangle was the girls' dormitory. It was called Elizabeth Waters. It was absolutely marvelous too.

And on campus the student union was also available for our use, and it was a tremendous place. So the four months in radio school at University of Wisconsin was excellent duty. Difficult, I mean, it was -- well, it had to come together because radio school was -- it takes a lot of practice and hard work. But it came together and in -- as a -- in an exam there they skimmed off about 12 of us that -- didn't tell us what we were going to do, but they just skimmed us off. And when we finished and the rest of the people went to the fleet, and we went on to a place so unknown to us on Bainbridge Island, Washington which then was the entry into what was then called ___+ attached, which is the Navy segment attached to the National Security Agency, which was a radio school to adapt what we had learned in our basic radio school to copying the Japanese code. That was highly secret, of course.

Prior to that assignment we'd undergone investigation back home, and this, of course, was absolutely top secret. At that time you kept your mouth shut and you never told anybody ever, even your spouses, presumably. Beg your pardon? Don't know. On proficiency, conceivably, but I was in the top class to begin with in radio school, but not all of us came out of that class that went on to intelligence school, and so I really don't know why they happened to pick the 12 of us, but they did.

But my class was -- I think was 300 guys -- 300 men, but there were only 12 of us that went onto Bainbridge. But that, again, was a very interesting school there, as it naturally would be. And learning to copy Japanese code -- and from there you were going to go -- nearly everybody was going to go to an overseas assignment. The worst conceivable assignment at that time appeared to be -- or we thought -- was probably Alaska, and if you caught Alaska, you caught the worst assignment there was. If you caught Australia, you caught the best, and there were others in the middle.

And after about three months there at Bainbridge, we were sent on to Wahiawa, Hawaii. So my arrival in Wahiawa, Hawaii, would be in late summer, as I recall -- in late summer of 1943. And then you just went through the rote of your duties there, which was not exciting, wasn't particularly exciting at all. You did eight hours on, eight off. Off time you were just eight on, eight off, eight on, eight off, eight on, eight off, no breaks. And depending upon just how intense the war was at that particular time, duty in Hawaii wasn't particularly difficult.

Naturally, you weren't getting shot at, and you're getting fed every day. You had a choice going in Wahiawa of two ways to get out of there. One of them was to go to DF duty. DF duty was Directional Finding. We had small Direction Finding installations in the islands out in the Pacific like Johnston, Palmyra, Guadalcanal, Wake. And then, of course, as the invasion started out there in the Gilberts and the Marianas and outlying islands, establishing DF sites there. Some fellows volunteered for that duty, and that didn't sound particularly interesting.

But task force duty sounded like the real great duty. That was going into the fleet on an admiral staff. There would be -- just a five-member group would go: a chief and four operators, along with a language officer. And, fortunately -- but you had to be selected based, again, on proficiency. And, fortunately, I got to go to task force in the fall of 1944.

Now, in June of 1944, my father died, was killed back in South Dakota. And, fortunately, I received an emergency leave, went back. And when I came back out into the fleet or came back out again -- back to Wahiawa -- I very much at that time, for whatever reason, wanted off the beach and wanted to get into the fleet. I wanted to get into the war. It probably was just the youth, being angry and what have you.

But what -- was assigned to a unit with Admiral Mitscher on the Bunker Hill and shipped out of Pearl on the Bunker Hill which was going to then be the invasion of, oh gracious -- see this followed the Marianas -- Iwo Jima, really. It was going to go into Iwo and also then Formosa when we were trying to retake Taiwan. I'll never forget when we first shipped out of Pearl, we were out a matter of days, and our language officer got a copy of the articles as to exactly what the battle plan was. And we were going to go up and bomb the island of Japan itself, and we could not conceive of that. This was absolute lunacy, it appeared to us.

Every ___ at that time thought the possibilities that we were going to survive were nil because it just did not make any sense to a raw young seaman like we were. But we went to Japan and did the bombing at that time, and from then on, for a period of about nine months, the duty was wartime and big time wartime.

Fortunately, I got off the Bunker Hill. A matter of days after I got off the Bunker Hill I was transferred over to the Yorktown on Admiral Radford's flag. Somebody was sick over there and -- oh, no, it was the chief. The chief was leaving, and I went over to relieve him. And as soon as I left, within a matter of days, the Bunker Hill took its big hit. I saw it happen. I saw the end itself, and wondered real quickly whether my crew or my poor friends that I'd left were alive or not. And it took a few days before I found that out, and that was a bad, bad hit. It took a torpedo, took a torpedo and was nearly destroyed. That particular raid is when the Franklin was hit also.

The Franklin burned up and then burned out. And the Bunker Hill and the Franklin were the two carriers --big carriers that took the big hits and took the big damage. Oh, yeah. It -- well, it was -- interesting thing when the unit we were in -- every morning, of course, you knew you were looking at -- you knew you were going to be under attack if you were in the area. We would be running there -- for a period of months we were running from Taiwan up to Kyushu. We would be running as hard as we could go through the course of the night towards Kyushu to get our planes off early in the morning and keep running still as hard as we could go to get them in for their bomb raids on Kyushu itself and then get close enough before they run out of gas to pick them up, turn around and head back to Taiwan to in turn do the same thing the following morning on Taiwan. So we went back and forth and back and forth. And so every morning you were going to be under attack.

And being a -- on intercept, what we did is -- is we were on the airways trying to pick up their aircraft and their communications on their aircraft. And, depending upon how loud the signal was and how many different operators there were, we could make a determination as to how far out the planes were and how many they were. And we in turn would then notify ___. And this went on until the planes came in picked up by radar and were getting closer and closer and then start their bomb runs on us. And there were days and days and days of that the pickets wouldn't get all of the -- the pickets wouldn't knock down all of the aircraft coming in and they would get inside the pickets and we saw a great deal of anti-aircraft firing from the carriers themselves.

It was -- oft times the aircraft could not ___ very high altitudes to stay opposite side of the -- as many guns as they could. So only the ?five inches? and things of that nature could possibly read them. And if they could get in over the pickets and get above us then they could do their diving on us. And it was just amazing as you would look out the portholes, and the Japanese aircraft every place and diving.And now the Bunker Hill, for instance, I can recall when one of them came down -- came down right on the water and then rather than being at a high elevation and diving, came down on the water and was skimming the water as it came in on its torpedo run. And there -- just lots -- there was just lots and lots of that. That was just an everyday situation.

And it -- we would have our radio equipment. If they were on voice, you could hear them yelling. And you'd have your equipment turned up as high as you could. You'd have -- on a -- on speaker, and you'd be on the telephone screaming a ___ plot, and the speaker would be screaming with the Japanese coming in, or you'd have it on code and they would -- the torpedo run was TOH TOH TOH TOH TOH TOH TOH. That was -- they sent the word to you. DIT DIT DAH DAH DIT DIT was TOH and it would be that DIT DIT DAH DAH DIT DIT or the bonsai DAH DIT DIT DIT. See DAH DIT DIT DAH DAH DIT DIT DAH DAH DIT DIT DAH.

And it would be screaming at you, and the planes would be diving, and the guns would be going off, and you're pointing at the planes that maybe your -- and maybe the quad right below your porthole didn't see and -- But you could hear them, and you knew they were there, and the gunners might not see them, so it was an interesting situation at times when you're screaming -- I can recall one time I had my head out the porthole and I had -- we had aircraft -- diving aircraft every place and one -- my -- a 40-millimeter quad right underneath our shack.

They didn't see; they were looking at something else. And I reached in my pocket, and I had a handful of change in there, and I threw a handful of change down on the 40 so they could turn up and look at me and see where I was pointing as we had this dive bomber coming in on us. And we're losing lots and lots of airplanes. ___+ airplanes are coming in to land shot up ___ rough seas coming in trying to land.

Our night fighters was a mess as they came in and -- in rough condition and would lose the right wing on the ?five inches? as they hit those spots and go spinning across the deck. Navy aviators had tough duty. They had really, really tough duty. And trying to find a way home any time they went anyplace. You try to find a way home, and you don't know whether your home still was there. It could have been hit and sunk. It could have been in trouble.

And you learn real fast that war isn't fun. That you grow up and with those guys that I went personally to radio school with -- University of Wisconsin -- and that I was with the whole time of my service. I grew up with them. I grew into manhood with them. I grew from a 17-year-old boy -- 17-year-old country boy into manhood. I remember them vividly. I learned much from them. Established friendships that are unbelievably valuable and solid to this day, and this is what, 50-some years later.

As a matter of fact, just 30 days ago I lost two of my closest friends of that particular time. Both of them and I started radio school with and had become very close to in recent years. One of those very good friends, David K. Naugle, recently died in Fort Worth, Texas very well voice -- well-known in Texas -- radio and television announcer -- very well-known all his life. Dave and I were roommates at University of Wisconsin radio school for a matter of days until they split us. But when we got to Wahiawa also after intelligence school Dave volunteered to go the DF route and I recall when we went to -- when I went into the fleetDave had come back from one of his DF duties back in the Gilberts and he went out on the invasion of Iwo.

And I can still remember that we're invading Iwo. I couldn't believe we were taking passes. The Navy fleet was taking passes close to the beach, and everything was shelling them. And pretty soon we had the carriers in this line going by as close to the beach as they could get and shelling the beach. Carriers, for God sakes, out there andthe admiral's sitting on the carrier and they wanted to get in that thing there so we're firing all the stuff we've got on them.I still remember that, and Dave and his group were trying to get a foothold on the beach at that time. They went in at that time of the invasion itself and secured our position there so that we would have the DF capability to assist in everything -- the direction finder units.

Because they could pick up any radio transmission of the aircraft -- Japanese aircraft and/or ships and for location purposes. And also if one of our aircraft would get lost -- and we did this often -- that they would get lost and tell where they were out in the Pacific, and I would come up on the frequency for identification we could pinpoint -- tell them exactly where they were, too.

But Dave and his group sat through at Iwo at that time, which was lousy duty. I think back as to food and eating and for some reason this became a problem. Getting to a meal was difficult, when there were only four of us in that shack, and we were under attack so much. You didn't want to leave your station, and I know we got coffee cans, and oft times we'd just send one guy down to chow hall and get soup in a coffee can. And rather than getting any food, that's all you'd get was soup, and you'd drink it out of a coffee can. I did too much of that because the minute the war was over my language officer, a tremendous lieutenant, sent me immediately to sick bay. And I weighed 112 pounds. And he said, "You get out of here." And he transferred me quick as he could get me out of there -- get me back out of the fleet, and he did because I was -- I guess I wasn't in too good shape that time. I had lost a lot. I had gone aboard weighing someplace around 155 and went down to 112 -- is a lot of weight loss, and it was principally just not getting down to the chow hall.

I remember any time that we'd be in the chow hall, somebody would get a little seasick. And you'd look for the new guys that had just come aboard. It's because they would be the first one's that you'd expect to get seasick. And I'd go down there, and I'd look for some new guy, and I'd go sit at his table. Because if his eyes started to cross, and he was going to get sick, and all of a sudden he jumped up and run, you'd grab his tray and then you'd get his food. And I could still think of that. Or you'd see some kid that was new, and you and your buddy would sit across from him and talk, and your conversation would be such to make him sick. And pretty soon his eyes would cross and away he'd go. And it would be a fight over getting his food.

You remember other things. I get a kick out of remembering Wednesday mornings. Wednesday morning was beans -- beans and donuts. That was the best breakfast we'd ever get. Can you imagine beans for breakfast? They were delicious. They were delicious, especially if you got a donut with them. And -- but you never got enough of that, especially if you wound up weighing 112 pounds ultimately. But Wednesday mornings were great. If I'd have got seven days of week of that, I wouldn't have lost the weight. One of the things that I found real interesting -- as we went further in the war our admirals -- ___+ we were on began to appreciate the intelligence that we could provide them more and more every day.

By the end of the war, whatever you said -- when I was with Mitscher, and also when I was with Radford -- especially Radford -- what you said was gospel. And -- but our organization, of course, had to prove itself. And right from the very beginning, of course -- right from Pearl Harbor we had to start proving ourselves. If they'd believed us at that time there wouldn't have been such a thing as Pearl Harbor. But they didn't believe what we had told them. And -- but I know as nothing but a white hat Admiral Radford was so courteous to me. And when I would talk to him in making great decisions about things as to what we could expect as far as air opposition, he really took ourinformation from our outfit to heart.

It was interestingto look back at it now and see the credence that was given to what nothing but enlisted men would have to tell him. I can think back to my first introduction to a Navy ship. Unfortunately, when I went to Bainbridge Island we rode the ferry back and forth from Seattle out to Bainbridge every day or whatever. We hit the beach, so that was my introduction to the open water. But then when we were transported from Treasure Island in San Francisco to Wahiawa, we were in a convoy of six LSTs.

And I want to tell you an LST is nothing good for -- to be used as a transport. That flat-bottomed tub rides like a stone sledge. LST: Landing Ship Tank. But it had -- I think they had four-decker bunks and here's all these -- tell all these troops of one nature or another that they're on, for instance, to Hawaii. And immediately when we -- the day that we were pulling out of San Francisco it was choppy.

The wind was -- pretty good wind that day, and it was choppy. So the bay was choppy, and those flat-bottom tubs start rolling, and the seasickness started and was unreal. Those kids would get seasick. They started vomiting, and some of them didn't quit vomiting. They were sick every minute they were on those tubs. And, naturally, when it starts the spell starts and they never could clean things up. So somebody's sick all the time, and down in those quarters -- those sleeping quarters -- it was horrible.Fortunately, I never got seasick ever. And I look back now, and I can still remember as we were pulling out of San Francisco, some of the guys that were on the fantail and got sick right there. And I can still remember the guys by names as their eyes turned crossed and they turned green and then their ___ started.

But that was a rough, rough trip for many guys -- their entrance to Navy duty. Just as far as being excited about -- well, the excitement was going overseas. When at long last -- when you've been in States and in training one ___ or another, and now you've got overseas orders. And so you go into the big, big, big place like Treasure Island. And -- but then there were thousands of people went through there every day and loaded on anything and everything that could float that was going out to sea, and so that was big. That was really big, leaving the States and going out to fight the big war. And, so it was exciting in that particular way, but it won't last you.

You felt like you were doing something, or you're going to do something rather than just being a student, so to speak, going through schools. So you're excited not -- because you know you're hading someplace to get into the big war. And until you've been in the big war, that's exciting. But as they say, you've been there once; don't need to do that again. You learn a lot. You learn a lot about wars. Well, the eating -- they tried to feed you. You heard things real early, like powdered eggs. You never heard of powdered eggs. Your mother never fed you powdered eggs. But you found out the Navy learned how. So you got your powdered eggs, and you got your cornflakes. And with your cornflakes you learned to look at it closely and take the black dead bugs and take them out. It was -- and, of course, the cooks didn't care. Their job was -- people were going to complain anyhow, so the cooks never gave any real concern about how bad the food was. And also I can -- and you learned --I learned right from my KP duty in boot camp something like this.

When you're going to have eggs there, they used real eggs. I still remember that. And I remember a guy sitting there in his jeans and breaking eggs and, I mean, it took hours, just breaking eggs in a great big vat. And he would first drop some of the shells and he just reached in with his hands and grabbed the shells and threw them out. And pretty soon he was going down deep and his shirtsleeves were soaked, also, with eggs. And he was doing something else and he'd come back and go back to breaking eggs and his hand's down in it again. He could care less what went in those eggs. And -- but you're going to eat them. They just didn't care. And that was the bad thing with food in the service.

On small boats it made a difference for then you had a direct relationship with your cook. ___+After -- when Dad was killed an I came back on emergency leave and went back out -- went back to Pearl again -- or went back to Treasure Island again -- and I think I was the only passenger on a net tender going back out to Pearl. And they were getting me on something quick to get me back to duty. And I went on this net tender, and they had one primary cook, and he was there. He was one of -- they were his friends because the number of a crew on a net tender aren't very many and so the food was ten times better because he cared about it.

But when you've got -- when you're cooking for a bunch of people that you don't know, whole different ballgame. Yorktown. Bunker Hill and the Yorktown. Yeah, I'm recording now. Well, I did ask Admiral Radford. When the war was over, that was Radford. What had happened was, as I said, I went out on the Bunker Hill and -- with Admiral Mitscher -- and the chief who was on the crew on the Yorktown -- it was time for him to go back to be rotated to go back to Pearl, back to PearlHarbor and -- so that when they were sending him back, theysent me over there. And I went over there until we got another man because -- and anyhow I just went from one plank to the other, and I was transferred at sea. Oh my god, that was interesting, being transferred at sea. Oh, good lord. I didn't know where we were.

We were in the North Pacific because it was cold water. Going to be transferred at sea. I'm sent down to the flight deck -- sorry, hangar deck of, you know, the Bunker Hill to be transferred over to an ammo ship. Let me think. It was an ammo ship, that's right, that was unloading ammunition at sea that we were taking on the Bunker Hill. They were doing it in a coal bucket which was maybe five feet long, three and a half feet wide and only maybe a foot deep and tied the four corners, of course, and swung over the side with the ammunition and unloaded and swung back -- the ammo ship. Anyhow, it came time after they finished -- and they had me sitting there waiting -- I had my sea bag what have you and it was time to put me -- to send me over. Not that they were going to put me in that ammo, whatever you want to call it, box or whatever.

They sent me in the littler thing and put my sea bag between my legs and started to swing me over the side. But the ships were all together.What they do is they're tied tight on one side on one ship to get the line is tied. On the other ship there's men on the line because as the ships rolled that -- the line has got to give -- has to slacken and then be tightened so you got men on it. Well, to make a long story short, they dumped me. I hit the water, and I went flat out of that thing, and I've got no life jacket.

Why I didn't drown, never know. Got picked up, fished out of that and -- by a destroyer -- and got taken back, put on again the ammo ship for the night and then got transferred the next day or two days later over on the Bunker Hill -- on the Yorktown. It was an absolute nightmare. They tried to drown me about three times on those various transfers. Put me in the mail sack, and it hit the water, and it was an absolute mess. How I got through it without being drowned, I'll still never know.

To somewhat clarify, on the first transfer from the Yorktown, they were going to put me on this ammo ship because Yorktown was in one carrier division and the Bunker Hill was in another one, so -- and they weren't going to meet. Things like an ammo ship that first dumped its ammo -- replenished ammo on the Bunker Hill and it was going to go to Yorktown. That's why I was to be put on it. But an ammo box is the box I described. It's maybe four by five feet square, and you'd put little shells or something in that box and then you'd pass it from one deck of one ship over to the other ship on this breeches buoy. And so it was supposed to be real simple that rather than sending ammo, after they got through passing the ammo,they'd put me in there and send me back over to the ammoship. Well, it's simple if you keep the doggone -- if you keep the line tight so that you don't drop the darn thing down in the middle so it hits the water.

But they didn't do a very good job. It hit the water, and it just catapulted me out of there -- fired me out of there. Well, that's, of course, big problems because a carrier is way, way, way too big to turn around looking for some poor sailor out there, and the ammo ship is the same way. So a destroyer, which was following, found me in not too long a time and fished me out. And so now I'm wet, and I'm on the destroyer. But the destroyer isn't going to -- over to the Yorktown either, so the destroyer has got to catch the ammo ship and transfer me back on it. And I think that was -- no -- I forgot what they put me in on that one. But, anyhow, I spent the night on that ammo ship and, of course, that's an experience too.

That ammo ship is not something you want to be on too well. That this is full of ammunition. If it gets under attack and gets hit it just wouldn't be boom and there's a hole in the ocean. And the Mount Hood had just gone up within a matter of days in ___ -- an ammo ship there. So we had learned all about ammo ships and what kind of duty it was. But, anyhow, I spent a sleepless night on that ship and then maybe it was a day or two days, maybe, until I get over to the Yorktown. Now they've got to figure out a way to get me to that ship -- on the Yorktown. I wasn't about to ride in a -- in another open ammunition box. No way. So they put -- and the mail because they also had the mail for the Yorktown. So they got a big mail sack. And the mail sack is -- maybe the diameter is 24 inches and about six feet deep. So, anyhow, they put me in this mail sack with my armson the outside, and they swing me across on that. Well, of course, it's deep, too. It was deeper than six feet deepbecause my feet didn't hit the bottom. So they swing me out to swing me back over, and the line goes slack again, and I hit the water again. But it got -- it picked up lots of water.

Fortunately, didn't go swimming again. But they drug me out of that and only got me over to the Bunker Hill and -- or to the Yorktown, and I had all of the transfers at sea that I was interested in for a while. There aren't many transfers at sea. I mean, there's a lot of it done, but the average sailor doesn't run into a situation like that. And crews usually don't make that kind of mistake, but when they're dealing with -- principally with material, they're nowhere near as careful with material as they need be but -- yet a human being. So they got a human being and sometimes they forget. And they didn't even know my name. (laughing) Oh, terrible.

It was icy cold, and it was the North Pacific. We were off Japan at that particular time, and it was cold. (laughing) You never know, you know. I had no idea. I know I was in there long enough that when the destroyer came alongside, they knew I'd been there a long time, and they knew that I wasn't going to last much longer. And I know they put a hook on -- they used a hook to dig me out of there and -- the hook at the back of my pants. And they drug me aboard, and they banged me up a little bit. But I was -- that made no difference. I was just happy to be there.

When I think back, for instance, about ___ shift back at Wahiawa, it's interesting as to how your radio shack was laid out. There might be 20 of us sitting at receivers -- radio receivers -- all copying different Japanese stations. Some of them might be weather stations; some of them are various fixed places ___+ Navy base has got a lot of encoded messages going out to the Japanese fleet wherever -- The interesting ones would be if you could catch -- if you could pick up a submarine and/or pick up ships at sea. And if you knew that it was a sub and/or a ship at sea, immediately notify your DF group for them to get a fix on it for its location.And in our -- for instance, in our radio shack there would be a few of us on what we called "search," and that would be the ones just kind of pick up the news stations. And then there would be -- the rest of the guys would be on fixed stations -- that when you came and sat down, you knew that you were going to be copying a particular station that was sending out it's general broadcast of the day. And -- but if you're on search, then you're sitting there just carefully twisting that dial.

Let's -- to give you an illustration, if, let us say you picked up a real guttural transmission, and you knew -- you could tell from its transmitter sound that it sounds like a submarine. You immediately yelled and notified to let a signal watch chief. And across the room on the other side are your DF operators, the guys working the DF frequencies. They would immediately -- you'd notify your chief what you're copying on which frequency. They would in -- very briefly on the -- the guys on the DF circuits would send out to all of the DF stations a notice to turn to a particular frequency like the one that you're copying and to get a fix on it. So your DF operator sitting there would notify the Wake and the Guadalcanal and the New Guinea and whatever stations and the Adak, Alaska and to copy a particular circuit or even particular frequency and a particular call sign. And they'd turn to it immediately, get a fix on it as to what the direction was from their location.

Then they would call it back in to these operators that were sitting in our shack -- that particular -- the fixes. Immediately, that information would go to other people in our section who would put it into information and set it on wire portal. No, not wire portal. What did we call them -- telex. Anyhow, it went on tape and immediately went to our headquarters in places like down in Pearl Harbor and in Washington D. C. for the cryptology people to put together to see what it was. But within a matter of minutes, if you picked up a -- as I said, a signal from something you thought was a submarine, within a matter of three minutes, all of your people would be -- all of your DF stations throughout the country would be on them on the same frequency, get a fix, and send it back.

And, as I said, again, within minutes it would be transcribed and forwarded on to higher headquarters for evaluation by them. The organization was amazing. You never -- we didn't know, at our level, what the overall result was. We didn't know what the cryptology -- what they were breaking down -- what they could easily break down and decode and what they couldn't. All you did was you followed their directions as to what stations they wanted you to keep copying, and that's what we did. So you're spending most of your time doing work that you didn't know the end result.

When you did learn the end result, some of the major things -- it tickled you to no end. Because you understood the rest of it had a purpose too, although there was no need for us to know what it was.I have no idea what this organization is doing at thistime. But we now know -- we didn't talk about NSA before. As for what organization we were in, we had various designations as to what that -- radio unit you were. But you were just radio; nothing had to do with intercept or anything of that nature. Now, of course, we know that we were an arm of NSA, and they still are, National Security Agency.

But now we also -- what has happened -- what is happening was technology -- it just kind of fascinates you as to what the organization could be doing today when they have technology. That from great distances away they can pick up conversations that they can see to -- that I can see -- hundreds of feet a way. When they have all of the -- all of it -- the technology today to be informed -- to be informed what somebody else is doing without their knowing that you're being informed. Naturally, that's what's happening throughout the world. How it's happening, I haven't the faintest idea.

The organization or the skill that I had at that time is really outmoded. Terribly, totally outmoded. Been replaced by high, high technology. When you think about the horrors of a war -- we talk about going into war now. We talk about the possibilities of problems with Iraq. And you think back to the days when you were vitally concerned and a part of that. I can remember during all of the time we'd be under attack at sea, you realize there's a difference between being under attack at sea and under attack on the land. It's not just hitting you. If you lose your platform -- if that ship is hit, even though you aren't hit, you're in big trouble. And that ship is awful big, so being hit by a bullet's one thing, but having the ship being hit by something to sink it is another thing. So you realize how valuable that ship is to protect your life.

I -- as an impressionable kid or whatever it was -- one of the reasons I lost the weight that I lost was I -- at sea I acquired a real identity that -- how important our job was. And I realized that this is no time for gold bricks. This was no time to be goofing off. This is serious time. And when I was on task force, I worked all the time. As a matter of fact, I went down and took my mattress off my assigned bunk down in whatever my sleeping quarters were and brought it up to our radio shack and put it underneath one of our positions. In other words, we had a metal -- see, it's called a metal table was what held our equipment. You didn't have desks as such, but metal tables. Underneath that you could put your mattress. And that's where I slept. I never left the shack.

And -- most of the guys did. They went down to their quarters when they were off, but I didn't. And if I was awake, I was on duty and -- because I just felt it was necessary. It's a whole ship -- involved an awful lot of men. One little slip and it could be a big, big, big disaster, and that was one of the reasons that I lost the weight that I did. That doing what I was supposed to do -- what I felt I was supposed to do -- was more important than going down to eat. And, naturally, they only fed you during certain hours. I wasn't real sure I was going to come out of there.

As a matter of fact, there are times when you're -- for some unexplainable reason, you absolutely believe that you're not going to make it, and there are other times that you think there is no way in the world you're going to die. And there were much more times that I thought there was no way in the world I was going to die. First of all, we were going to beat them at their own game, that I could do my job better than the Japanese could do, and it was all a situation of just going through the amount of time to get the job done and to get home and get out of here.

But there are times when you're under attack that you cannot believe what devastation there is. The -- on a daily basis their craft would come back and there'd be the kills. And over the squawk box you'd hear how many aircraft we got that particular day: how many our fighter planes had knocked down and how many our ship had knocked down. And you listened to that over and over again day after day after day. And you look out -- you look out during some of those attacks, and you see some of our ships being hit or after attack the smoke coming from the ships that'd been hit. And you realize -- matter of time that they can get you too.

And it's an amazing thing, but you just keep going. Cross your fingers. Not much of a choice, but you just keep going. But then you get to a time like now, and I look back, and I say, "Why, why?" It would appear to me that if I look at any country -- nearly any country in the world, there's a fellow just like me, about my age, got the same kind of family I got. He doesn't know me and I don't know him, and he doesn't want to kill me. I don't want to kill him. That's the situation, I'm sure, in Iraq, Saudi Arabia, North Korea, the Sudan, Ivory Coast, Palastine, all the countries of the world. And I say, "How does this happen? How does this happen?" I am certain that there's my counterpart in these countries, and they don't know me, and they don't hate me. They don't want to kill me, but we wind up in wars.

And I -- I remember the day the war was over. Our shack -- our radio shack was right off the captain's catwalk, right above the hangar deck. You come out of our shack and you're pretty much -- you hit the catwalk, and you're looking down on the hangar deck. ___+ There was a first aid station that was being -- was converted to a shack for us on ___ carrier. But, anyhow, the day the war was over I can remember coming out of -- when I heard it -- when we heard it I came out of the shack, and I'm standing, I'm looking down at these idiots down on the hangar deck running around like crazy, hugging each other and yelling. Just running around and yelling, tickled to death.

The situation -- we're going home. An amazing thing is that the flow of the conversation was not "the war is over," it's -- it was "we're going home" that was important. You just got to drop the word "war." It wasn't even the thought of there's no more shooting or anything like that. It was -- going home was the important thing.

Well, anyhow, as I said, they sent me down to sick bay immediately and found out I weighed 112 pounds and did whatever, ran an examination on me and decide to get me back out of there as quick as they could. And then they come up with a point system, of course, within a matter of days as to discharge us. And I had enough points to get me and another guy out based on my service and time in the front lines and things of that nature. But I was in the regular Navy because I stayed, and I joined the USN. And my hitch wasn't up because the war was over one fall -- VJ Day, and I -- my hitch was not over until the day I was 21, which was -- the day before I was 21, which would be the 20th of January.

So, anyhow, they get me out of there pretty soon and send me back to Pearl, and I get back to Pearl and, fortunately, they immediately sent me back to the States. I had to just wait around there in my station at Wahiawa. I don't know why -- for just about four or five days, and they brought me another ship to send me back to the States. And then I went back to Bainbridge Island to stay there for two months by -- there was two months left when I got there until discharge time.

And -- but here I am, I'm 21 years of age, didn't have the faintest idea of where I was going in this world. I was a 17-year-old small-town kid going in and not 21 years old. And, in the meantime, of course, I'd lost a father and had a mother and little kid sister and two other minor -- daughter -- minors as sisters -- but -- back in Rapid City that had to be taken care of. My mother was getting my allotment, so she was getting most of my money. And -- but, anyhow, I'm going back and had absolutely no particular goals at that time.

Oh, wait a second, we did too -- we used to talk about when we -- I remember something. We all once -- we made a pact -- a bunch of us -- that we were going to meet at Arizona State -- all go to school there because we were going to the biggest party school in the country. That's right. We were all going to meet there in the fall, in the fall of '45 and go to school at ASU because that, supposedly, was the big party school. But it worked out none of them was there. Nobody went to ASU. We all went back home and then got lined out one way or the other.

Some people got right into a job that they kind of liked, got married, or something established -- obligations which then controlled them. Fortunately, I got back and asked enough questions to learn how to get into college and started college right away and to get an education. But when I went in the Navy, had absolutely no idea how they were going to get an education -- never really thought that much about it because I just -- I had no idea how to get into college let alone how much it cost or anything else. But the GI Bill was just absolutely tremendous in the advantages that it made available to all of us. I think often about, also, the good fortune I had in being in this organization.

The quality of personnel in that organization was excellent. We had very few bruisers, so to speak. This was a real fine bunch of fellows. Their ability to learn -- just a high-class bunch of fellows. And through the course of life that's been proven -- been established. It was -- and from them I learned a great deal. I -- it was those fellows that helped me grow up. They grew up with me. It was from them I learned and adopted much of my demeanor, my persona. It was great. It was a great educational experience by some great teachers. I value that time I spent in the service.

But I was one of the fortunate ones. There were an awful lot that weren't that fortunate, and I always keep that in mind, that my perspective is very limited. I don't speak for everybody at that age and at that time. It's very personal with every individual. It wasn't anything general, as such, and I feel lucky that I came home in one piece.
